reason: Petioluliform says a leaflet or blade base narrows into a stalk like a petiolule. FLOPO clawed (unguiculate) is the petal term for an abrupt claw. The earlier rules for the same idea used other terms: petiolelike went to attenuate (R0804) and falsely petiolate to tapered (R0912). With only 5 statements and no way to tell an abrupt narrowing from a gradual one, no single term is safe.

This is treated like 'tinged with pink' (R0984), 'tinged purple' (R1031) and 'tinged brown' (R0991), which were mapped to the plain colour. 'Suffused' only says how strong the colour is, and that goes in the record as a degree word.
FLOPO_0991024 ovate is defined as a 2-D outline broadest below the middle. 'Widest proximal (to middle)' fits flat parts. On a fruit or seed the same words mean ovoid.

Indented means notched but does not say where, so emarginate (notched at the apex) is too narrow. 'Not notched' (R1212) covers the apex notch of the examples, and an emarginate apex is still a kind of notch. The region goes in the region slot when it is stated.

Vespertine flowers open at dusk and stay open through the night, so anthesis does happen in darkness. PATO nocturnal fits this. PATO crepuscular (PATO_0095005) would wrongly add dawn. The narrower evening timing is lost, but the statement stays true.
FLOPO_0991025 obovoid is a 3-D shape. On a leaf or petal, 'broadest near summit' means obovate (PATO_0001936). So the rule is only right for solid parts.
Pachycaul means having a thick stem. Increased thickness (synonym stout) is right only on the stem. On 'whole plant' it would say the whole plant is thick, so the stem has to be the bearer.

This is read the same way as 'not visible' (R0067), 'obscure' and 'indistinct'. Veins or features that are 'not discernible' are taken as not clearly visible. A rule cannot safely claim they are absent.

In botany recurved is the usual word for styles and phyllary tips that curve outward and back, away from the axis. PATO has no 'curved outward', and spreading (PATO_0104356) does not say the part is curved.

A spicate panicle (mostly in grasses) is a contracted panicle that looks like a spike, so FLOPO spike-like describes its overall form. The examples do not describe a mix of two forms. This follows 'spicately arranged' (R1435).
'Uniting' said of petals, filaments or sepals means fusing, which is connate (FLOPO_0991067; see 'partially united' R1096). Only for veins does it mean anastomosing.

'Without basal glands' says the glands are missing only at the base. The rule would say the gland is absent from the whole bearer, which can be false. Absence in one region needs the region-of-the-bearer pattern, not a quality rule.
PATO_0000947 elliptic has ellipsoid as an exact synonym. 'Long-' is a degree word, handled like 'narrowly ellipsoid' (R0295) and 'narrow-elliptic' (R0346). A stated ratio goes to pattern 11.

The endostome sticks to the exostome without being fused, which is FLOPO adherent. The other part goes in the 'towards' slot of docs/odp/09, as was ruled for 'not adherent' (R0928) and 'weakly adherent' (R1652).

A densiflorous inflorescence has its flowers closely packed. PATO condensed ('more closely packed together') on the inflorescence covers this, as with the earlier mapping of compact inflorescences to condensed. The flowers are implied because the bearer is the inflorescence.

The quality belongs to the leaf sinus (PO_0025384), but the rule sets only the quality. Decreased width would land on the leaf or lobe, which are not narrow. This needs the sinus to be put in as the bearer (part-of-bearer pattern), not a quality rule.

'Composite' is ambiguous. In French floras 'composées' (leaves) means compound, and in English it can mean compound or Asteraceae-like. As a quality word it would put a capitulum on leaves and other parts.

The thin part is the fruit valve (PO_0000033), but the rule would put decreased thickness on the whole fruit, which would mean a flattened fruit. The valve has to be put in as the bearer (part-of-bearer pattern); a quality rule cannot do that.

The Plant Ontology defines awn (PO_0025349) only as an appendage of a glume, lemma or palea. 'Bristle-tipped' was mapped to awn present (R0128) for these parts. On leaves, bracts or teeth a bristle tip is not an awn.
PO_0020139 leaf midvein (synonym midrib) fits leaves only. On stipules, sepals, bracts or fruit valves the bearer should be vascular bundle (PO_0005020), as the notes to R1472 and R1773 say.

This follows 'without keel' (R0640) and 'without keels' (R0830): the lemma and glume keel is a ridge (carinate = keel-shaped), so its absence is 'not keel-shaped'. PO keel (PO_0025327) is the papilionaceous petal pair and cannot be used. 'Abaxial' goes in the region slot.

PATO elliptic has ellipsoid as an exact synonym, and 'broadly' and 'narrowly ellipsoid' (R0039, R0295, R1367) were all mapped to it. A short ellipsoid is barely longer than wide, so prolate (polar axis longer) adds an elongation the word plays down. R1316 broad-ellipsoid → prolate is the outlier.

The hair covering is puberulous, and 'granular' describes a minute surface roughness of the hairs or surface. It is handled like 'granular-papillose' → papillose (R1072). The extra texture is a cue, not a separate class.

A slipper-shaped (calceolate) lip or petal is a deep pouch. FLOPO saccate ('shaped like a pouch or bag') is the existing, broader term. There is no calceolate class, and one is not needed for this number of statements.
'Sparsely' is a density degree word, dropped as in 'sparsely pubescent' (R0080) and 'sparsely leafy' (R0400). The value hirsute stays true.
Indistinct veins, costae or markings are inconspicuous, as ruled for 'indistinct' and 'obscure'. Elsewhere 'unclear' often describes the text or the identity of a taxon, not a visible feature.
This is the same as the reviewed rule 'pale chestnut-brown' → chestnut colour (R0751). 'Pale' is a lightness cue and goes in the record.

This is 'glandular-setulose' (R0663) with the words in the other order: small bristles tipped with glands. FLOPO glandular-pubescent is defined as at least some hairs being gland-tipped, which covers it.
This follows 'white powdery' (R1270) and 'white-farinose' (R1972). White is the colour of the powder, not of the bearer, so mealy alone is the correct statement.
FLOPO equal is the size quality of a set of like parts. 'Equal in length' (R0163), 'equal length' (R0213) and 'equal-length' (R1165) already map to it.
